newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin sees strongest economy in years.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin sees strongest economy in years.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Monday that Canada was on the brink of its best economic performance since World War Two.

"We are on the brink...of what is going to be one of the strongest periods of sustained growth and progress that this country has had since the end of the Second World War," Martin told a luncheon sponsored by the Quebec MBA Association.
Martin cited declines in Canada's government deficit and interest rates as causes for his optimism .

Martin noted that foreign portfolio investment in Canada rose over the past four months, but said Canada would have truly succeeded only when it became the export center for foreign companies investing in the country.
In reply to an audience question, Martin again ruled out any across-the-board tax cuts to take advantage of Canada's lower deficit and interest rates.
Martin said that a tax cut now would result in "a massive" tax increase two years down the road.
"We will have lost everything we've gained to this point," he said.
Martin added that the political uncertainty surrounding the Quebec government's separatist policy hindered investment and job growth in Canada.
Martin said he would prefer that Quebec not hold another referendum on sovereignty for at least 10 years, if at all.
"For me, 10 years would be the minimum. I would prefer not having a referendum at all," Martin said.
The Parti Quebecois government in Quebec has said that it would hold another referendum on sovereignty if it won the next provincial election, which could be held as late as 1998.

Martin told reporters afterward that he expected job growth in Canada to pick up due to consistent reductions in interest rates over the past year and a half. But he noted that there was traditionally a one to two-year lag between interest rate cuts and accelerated job creation.

"This interest rate reduction only really began a little under a year ago, the major move. We are already beginning to see it (job growth), but it's quite clear that it's going to pick up as time goes on," Martin said.
